edition.title: P100 NEWS + CULTURE
edition.deck: War and energy pressures, political choices and public services shape today’s agenda, alongside reporting on communities facing immediate change.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises consequential developments across international affairs and the UK, while giving Denmark coverage to substantial policy, safety and public-service stories. Related reports are grouped; allegations and unresolved questions remain attributed.

content.headline: Russia strikes a second major bridge in Kyiv, mayor says
content.shortHeadline: Russia strikes second major Kyiv bridge, mayor says
content.standfirst: Mayor Vitali Klitschko says a strike damaged the Northern Bridge, blocking traffic across it. The attack follows repeated strikes on another key crossing, adding pressure to the capital’s transport links.

image.caption: Kyiv’s Northern Bridge, which the mayor said was hit in a Russian strike.

sources.originalTitle: Russia strikes second major bridge in Kyiv, mayor says

segments.body: A Russian strike hit Kyiv’s Northern Bridge on Saturday morning, damaging the road surface and trolleybus overhead wires, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said. Traffic from the left bank to the right bank was blocked as emergency services responded.

segments.title: A series of attacks
segments.body: The strike followed repeated drone attacks on the Southern Bridge since Thursday. Both crossings link eastern and western parts of the capital. After the earlier strikes, Klitschko said the city was in a “very dramatic situation” and its defence council held a crisis meeting.

content.headline: Christa Pike remains critically ill after failed Tennessee execution
content.shortHeadline: Christa Pike critically ill after failed execution
content.standfirst: Pike’s lawyers say the death-row inmate is unconscious and on a ventilator after two doses of pentobarbital failed to kill her. Tennessee has halted executions for the rest of the year and ordered an independent review.

image.caption: Christa Pike was due to be executed in Tennessee, where the attempt failed.

source.credit: Foto: J. Miles Cary / Ritzau Scanpix

sources.originalTitle: US murderer Christa Pike unconscious and on ventilator after failed execution, lawyers say
Kvinde i respirator efter mislykket henrettelse
I've seen nearly 500 executions - but never one like Christa Pike's

segments.body: Christa Pike, 50, remained critically ill in hospital on Thursday night, unconscious and on a ventilator, according to court filings by her lawyers. They say prison officials administered two doses of pentobarbital during Wednesday’s execution attempt, but she survived and was taken to hospital.

segments.title: Questions about the procedure
segments.body: Pike’s lawyers allege that staff repeatedly failed to place intravenous lines correctly and did not realise the veins had ruptured. Tennessee’s corrections department has defended its protocol, while Governor Bill Lee ordered an independent review and halted executions in the state for the year. Authorities have not said whether they will try again.

segments.title: A rare outcome
segments.body: Veteran execution reporter Michael Graczyk, who has covered nearly 500 executions in Texas, told the BBC he had never seen one fail after the drug was delivered. He said the incident raised questions about a protocol that does not specify what happens if a person is still alive after its second dose.

perspectives.body: Graczyk places Pike’s survival in the context of decades of lethal-injection reporting: he recalls needle problems, but says he has never witnessed an execution fail after the injection.

content.headline: G7 agrees to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel
content.shortHeadline: G7 to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel
content.standfirst: The coordinated release is intended to ease supply concerns after US President Donald Trump threatened an export ban. Diesel prices remain high, and the scale and timing of individual countries’ contributions are not yet clear.

image.caption: Diesel prices in the UK have reached a record average, according to RAC figures.

sources.originalTitle: G7 to release millions of barrels of oil and diesel after Trump threat
Truckers plea for fuel duty bailout as diesel prices hit record high
Petulant Trump will feel empowered by world’s latest surrender to his demands

segments.body: G7 leaders agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel through the International Energy Agency over four months, including a substantial diesel release in the first 20 days. Members also agreed not to restrict energy exports between them, after Trump threatened to ban US diesel exports.

segments.title: Prices and supply remain uncertain
segments.body: The agreement is intended to calm markets, but it does not resolve the underlying supply pressures. The UK’s average diesel price reached a record 200.01p a litre, according to RAC figures reported by the i Paper. The G7 has not yet set out which partner countries will contribute stocks or how quickly they will do so.

segments.title: A short-term buffer
segments.body: Supply-chain expert Jonathan Owens said emergency stocks could ease immediate pressure and give businesses time to adapt, but drawing them down leaves less protection against future disruption until reserves are replenished. An i Paper columnist argued the deal also showed Trump’s ability to pressure allies; that is an opinion, not a G7 finding.

perspectives.body: The i Paper’s analysis frames the release as a political win for Trump and warns that depleted reserves may leave allies more exposed later. This is the columnist’s interpretation of the agreement.

content.headline: French education protests disrupt hundreds of schools as clashes continue
content.shortHeadline: French school protests spread as police clash with students
content.standfirst: Demonstrations over staffing, overcrowded classrooms and school conditions have disrupted hundreds of schools. Authorities report arrests and injuries as the protests spread, while the government says violence has overtaken the original student demonstrations.

image.caption: A fire burns in a street during student protests in Brest.

sources.originalTitle: Riot police clash with students as education protests rage in France
Skoleelever over hele Frankrig demonstrerer
School protests send shivers down French government's spine

segments.body: Protests over education standards have affected 735 of France’s 3,700 schools, according to Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said 1,747 people were arrested on Friday. Police clashed with demonstrators as fires and damage were reported in several cities.

segments.title: Demands and disorder
segments.body: Students have cited too few teachers, crowded classrooms and run-down buildings; planned budget cuts have also fuelled anger. The education ministry said at least 65 staff were injured. Ministers say non-students have joined the protests, while unions have backed the students’ right to demonstrate.

segments.title: Political claims disputed
segments.body: BBC correspondent Hugh Schofield’s analysis says some opponents fear the protests are being manipulated by the hard left; the France Unbowed party denies doing more than supporting a legitimate movement and has urged students to avoid violence. Schofield also notes that the unrest comes months before a presidential election.

perspectives.body: The BBC analysis focuses on the political risks for the government and the disputed claim that the hard left is exploiting the protests. France Unbowed rejects that accusation.

content.headline: Spain’s government loses housing votes after protests over evictions
content.shortHeadline: Spain’s government loses key housing votes
content.standfirst: Parliament rejected two measures intended to protect tenants, a setback for Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez amid a broader housing crisis. The defeat has revived speculation about an early election, but his government has not announced its next step.

image.caption: Demonstrators react in Spain’s parliament after a housing vote.

sources.originalTitle: Spanish PM Sánchez loses key housing crisis vote after eviction of woman, 87
Boligkrisen har sendt spaniere på gaden - nu kan den føre til tidligt valg, vurderer korrespondent

segments.body: Spain’s Congress rejected two government decrees aimed at addressing the housing crisis. The measures included protections for vulnerable tenants, lease extensions and restrictions on some property purchases. The votes followed protests after 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her Madrid home.

segments.title: A political setback
segments.body: The defeat underlined that Sánchez’s minority government lacks a parliamentary majority and increased speculation that he could call an early election. Spanish media reported that the government would consider its next move over the weekend; no decision had been announced in the gathered reports.

segments.title: Dispute over the proposed remedies
segments.body: The conservative People’s Party and Vox opposed both decrees, while Together for Catalonia’s opposition helped ensure they failed. Sánchez argued the measures were necessary to bring order to the housing market; critics said they were rushed and could have unintended effects.

content.headline: Bangkok floods kill about 40 as rain overwhelms the Thai capital
content.shortHeadline: Bangkok floods kill 40 as water overwhelms the city
content.standfirst: Flooding submerged neighbourhoods, disrupted transport and forced thousands into shelters after exceptionally heavy rain. Scientists say extreme rainfall in the region is a growing risk, but say it is too early to attribute these particular downpours to climate change.

sources.originalTitle: Bangkok at breaking point as floods turn streets into stagnant lakes

segments.body: About 40 people died in flood-related incidents in Bangkok, including drownings and accidental electrocutions, according to the government. Thousands stayed in more than 230 shelters. In some parts of the city, around 300mm of rain fell in roughly two days, leaving streets and neighbourhoods under water.

segments.title: City life disrupted
segments.body: Flooding affected the main airport, contributed to flight cancellations and left luggage piled up; many schools closed and traffic gridlocked. The government declared a disaster across all 50 districts. Bangkok relies on canals, pumps and dikes, but extensive construction has reduced parts of the canal network.

segments.title: A changing rainfall risk
segments.body: An ocean scientist told the Guardian that long-term models point to more intense rainfall in the region. The particular event was linked to a low-pressure system that stalled over Bangkok; the report says it is too early to attribute these rains specifically to climate breakdown, and notes the influence of El Niño complicates the picture.

perspectives.body: The report distinguishes the immediate weather system behind this flood from the longer-term climate trend: scientists see a regional increase in extreme rainfall, but have not attributed this event to climate change.

content.headline: Oil exports from the Middle East recover despite Hormuz risks
content.shortHeadline: Middle East oil flows near pre-war levels despite Hormuz risk
content.standfirst: Data from Kpler shows regional oil flows reached 92% of their pre-war baseline in the final week of September, despite continuing threats to shipping. Analysts point to pipelines, US support for vessels and ship-to-ship transfers, but question how sustainable these workarounds are.

sources.originalTitle: Three reasons Middle East oil supply is nearly back to pre-Iran war levels

segments.body: Middle East oil flows reached 92% of their pre-war baseline in the final week of September, according to maritime intelligence firm Kpler. The Strait of Hormuz remains restricted, and an average of 12 million barrels a day passed through it during the week to 30 September, compared with a pre-war 17 million.

segments.title: Routes around the strait
segments.body: Kpler says about 40% of the region’s oil exports in September bypassed Hormuz using overland pipelines. More than 60 large tankers have also been moving oil through a shuttle system, with transfers to other vessels in the Gulf of Oman. US forces have supported ships passing through the strait since at least mid-June.

segments.title: A fragile recovery
segments.body: The report says successful Iranian attacks on commercial shipping were at their highest since March. Analysts warn that the workarounds could be vulnerable to further attacks or a change in US policy. Oil products and liquefied natural gas exports also remain well below pre-conflict levels, and Iranian exports have nearly stopped under a US blockade.

content.headline: Ukraine races to intercept faster Russian attack drones
content.shortHeadline: Ukraine develops faster interceptors for Russia’s new drones
content.standfirst: Ukrainian firms are testing interceptor drones against Russia’s faster, jet-powered Geran models. The contest is moving quickly, and analysts say interceptors are only one part of a broader defence system.

image.caption: Wreckage of a Russian attack drone after a raid in Ukraine.

sources.originalTitle: How Ukraine is taking down Putin’s deadly new drones

segments.body: Ukrainian drone maker Wild Hornets says its Sting S interceptor has destroyed several Russian Geran-5 drones and about a dozen slower Geran-4s during combat testing. The company plans mass production after testing is complete. Other Ukrainian systems are also being tested in the field.

segments.title: A rapid cycle of adaptation
segments.body: Ukraine’s military intelligence says the Geran-5 can travel at up to 370mph and carry a warhead weighing about 90kg. Analysts told the i Paper that faster drones and more complex electronics require more sophisticated responses, while new interceptor designs can become outdated as targets change.

segments.title: More than one answer
segments.body: Defence analyst Sam Cranny Evans cautioned that interceptor drones are part of a larger system, not a stand-alone solution. Another analyst argued that striking launch sites inside Russia could also be important. Wild Hornets says its AI supports human operators rather than carrying out fully automatic interceptions.

content.headline: Poll finds 49% support rejoining EU as Labour weighs its next move
content.shortHeadline: Poll finds 49% back rejoining the EU
content.standfirst: A survey of 11,461 people found more support for rejoining than opposition, and suggested closer EU ties could boost Labour’s vote share. The figures come as ministers remain divided over the political risks of reopening the Brexit debate.

image.caption: A pro-EU campaigner calls for the UK to rejoin the bloc.

sources.originalTitle: Half of UK wants to rejoin EU and backing it could drive up Labour vote, megapoll finds

segments.body: A Messina Group poll found 49% of respondents supported rejoining the EU and 28.5% opposed it. The survey of 11,461 people was conducted from 12 to 24 September. It also found 52.4% thought leaving the EU had been wrong, compared with 29.7% who thought it right.

segments.title: Different routes to closer ties
segments.body: The poll found support for several other options too, including cutting trade barriers while keeping the current relationship and joining a customs union. A plurality wanted immediate rejoining, while opinions differed on whether a referendum, a general election mandate or a parliamentary decision should settle the question.

segments.title: Political calculation and caution
segments.body: The Guardian reports that its poll modelling suggested closer-ties proposals could lift Labour’s vote share by between 4.3 and 7.4 points. Some Labour ministers and MPs remain wary that a renewed Brexit argument could benefit Reform and reopen divisions in leave-voting constituencies.

content.headline: Man accused of Ann Widdecombe’s murder charged with terror preparation
content.shortHeadline: Widdecombe murder suspect charged over alleged terror plans
content.standfirst: Police say Joshua Kerry faces a further charge of preparing terrorist acts, including acts allegedly directed against Nigel Farage. The charge relates to alleged activity between 2024 and 2026; the case is continuing and the allegations have not been proved.

image.caption: Joshua Kerry at Westminster magistrates’ court in July.

sources.originalTitle: Ann Widdecombe murder suspect charged with planning terror act against Nigel Farage
Widdecombe suspect charged with planning terror act against Farage

segments.body: Joshua Kerry, 28, has been charged with one count of preparing terrorist acts, counter-terrorism police said. The alleged activity took place between 31 May 2024 and 8 July 2026 and included plans against Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, according to the charge. Kerry is also accused of murdering Ann Widdecombe.

segments.title: Security questions
segments.body: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said the new charge raised serious questions about the security of MPs and others in public life. A representative of the Jo Cox Foundation said threats and intimidation can endanger individuals and their families and called for stronger prevention and protection.

segments.title: Separate investigation
segments.body: The Guardian reports that a previously closed investigation into an alleged firebomb attack at Farage’s home was reopened in August. Police said they had identified a line of inquiry that may have been relevant but was not pursued at the time. The report does not establish a connection between that investigation and the new charge.

content.headline: London council warns it may need a 150% council tax rise
content.shortHeadline: Hammersmith and Fulham warns of possible 150% tax rise
content.standfirst: Hammersmith and Fulham says a steep rise in its council-tax element could be needed to balance its budget in 2027–28 after central government funding is cut. The council’s report presents it as a scenario, not a confirmed increase.

image.caption: The government’s funding rules are at the centre of the council’s warning.

sources.originalTitle: London Labour council warns it may raise council tax by 150%

segments.body: A report due to be published by Hammersmith and Fulham council says a 150% increase in its council-tax element would broadly balance the budget on current assumptions. For a Band D household, it would add £29.11 a week in 2027–28, excluding the Greater London Authority precept.

segments.title: Funding dispute
segments.body: The council says its government funding will fall from £150.5m in 2025–26 to £72.4m over four years under the funding settlement. Ministers say the formula redirects money towards places with greater need and note that local authorities decide their own council-tax levels.

segments.title: Other scenarios
segments.body: The report also sets out 100% and 125% increases, which would still leave budget gaps of £46.1m and £20.6m respectively. The council argues its deprivation and cost-cutting record should be recognised; the government says councils should put taxpayers first.

content.headline: Manchester City case puts Andy Burnham’s ties to owners under scrutiny
content.shortHeadline: Manchester City ruling puts Burnham’s ties under scrutiny
content.standfirst: Manchester City denies wrongdoing and says it will appeal a commission’s findings of financial-rule breaches. Reporting also raises questions about Andy Burnham’s praise for the club’s owners and a private government meeting with its chairman shortly before the ruling.

image.caption: An illustration about Andy Burnham’s comments on Manchester City’s owners.

sources.originalTitle: How Man City’s owners wooed Andy Burnham, from property deals to football chats
No 10 feels heat on Man City scandal after private trade talks with Abu Dhabi
Manchester City’s guilty verdict brings football’s great sell-off crashing to earth

segments.body: A Premier League commission found Manchester City guilty of 114 charges relating to financial misconduct, including allegations that “sham” sponsorship deals concealed funding. The club denies wrongdoing and plans to appeal. The outcome of the appeal and any sanction remain unresolved.

segments.title: Political ties and a meeting
segments.body: The i Paper reports that Prime Minister Andy Burnham praised Abu Dhabi’s owners for investing in Manchester when discussing the case, then No 10 stressed that no one was above the rules. It also reports that City chairman Khaldoon al-Mubarak met Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds on 14 September; officials said the meeting covered UK-UAE relations, not Manchester City.

segments.title: The wider argument over ownership
segments.body: A Guardian columnist argues that the ruling should prompt wider scrutiny of football’s commercialisation and ownership model, while also acknowledging the investment’s role in Manchester’s development. That is the columnist’s analysis; City’s appeal means the commission’s findings are not the final word.

perspectives.body: The Guardian columnist places the case within a broader critique of football’s sale to wealthy investors, contrasting the commercial gains with supporters’ traditions and the idea of clubs as shared civic institutions.

content.headline: Burnham plans legislation to change pension triple lock before 2030
content.shortHeadline: Pension triple lock change to be legislated before 2030
content.standfirst: The government says the earnings element will be adjusted to limit unusually large increases, while the guarantee remains in place until 2030. The proposed savings are uncertain and will depend on future economic conditions.

image.caption: Andy Burnham announced plans for a national care service alongside the pension changes.

sources.originalTitle: Burnham to pass law scrapping pension triple lock before next election
Badenoch wants to save the Triple Lock. But senior Tories want it gone

segments.body: Andy Burnham says the state pension triple lock will remain until 2030, but the government intends to legislate during this parliament to change how the earnings element works. The current guarantee raises pensions by the highest of inflation, earnings growth or 2.5%.

segments.title: Savings are uncertain
segments.body: The government estimates the adjustment could reduce annual pension spending by £15bn by the end of the 2030s and £50bn by 2050. The Resolution Foundation says estimates vary widely depending on the period used to model earnings and inflation, and that the savings are difficult to predict.

segments.title: Political debate
segments.body: Burnham says the changes would help fund a national care service in England. Some unions and opposition parties criticise changing the guarantee, while YouGov polling cited by the Guardian found 48% supported Burnham’s plan and 28% opposed it. The Conservatives remain publicly committed to the triple lock, despite internal debate about its long-term cost.

content.headline: England’s school inspection system to be overhauled again
content.shortHeadline: Ofsted inspections face another overhaul in England
content.standfirst: Education Secretary Lucy Powell wants Ofsted to reconsider how its new ratings system accounts for schools’ social and economic circumstances. Leaders say the framework is causing stress and may disadvantage schools serving pupils with greater needs.

image.caption: Powell wants Ofsted to reconsider how inspections assess inclusion.

sources.originalTitle: England school inspections to be overhauled again after barrage of complaints

segments.body: Lucy Powell plans to ask Ofsted to revise aspects of its new inspection framework, particularly how it measures inclusion and accounts for pupils’ backgrounds. The report-card system, introduced last year, replaced single headline grades with ratings across six areas; Powell has not proposed scrapping it.

segments.title: Concerns from schools
segments.body: The National Association of Head Teachers says inspection must take account of the different challenges schools face. A National Education Union survey cited by the Guardian found two-thirds of respondents thought the new system was as bad as or worse than its predecessor, and three-quarters said it had harmed their mental health.

segments.title: Questions about fairness
segments.body: A study by former inspector Steve Wren found lower ratings among schools with more pupils receiving free school meals or additional learning support, and raised questions about whether prior attainment is adequately considered. Ofsted has commissioned an independent evaluation, with an interim report due later this year.

content.headline: Bluetongue outbreak reaches record levels and spreads to Scotland
content.shortHeadline: Bluetongue outbreak is worst on record for UK farms
content.standfirst: Defra has recorded 2,201 cases of bluetongue so far this season, already exceeding the previous three seasons combined. The livestock disease has reached Aberdeenshire, and farmers say obtaining vaccines is challenging.

image.caption: Bluetongue is spread by midges and has been detected in UK livestock.

sources.originalTitle: Worst ever outbreak of bluetongue hits British farms

segments.body: Defra has recorded 2,201 bluetongue cases since the season began on 1 July, including 1,103 in September. A case means a premises with at least one affected animal, so the number of animals infected is likely higher. The disease has reached Scotland for the first time and been found as far north as Aberdeenshire.

segments.title: Pressure on farms
segments.body: Bluetongue affects sheep and cattle and can cause fever, ulcers, swelling and lameness; severe cases can be fatal. It does not affect people or food safety. The National Farmers’ Union says farmers face constant monitoring, and that access to vaccines has been challenging.

segments.title: Climate link
segments.body: The report says hotter conditions can help the virus develop in midges, which transmit it. The World Organisation for Animal Health links the spread of bluetongue in Europe to climate breakdown. A climate analyst called this outbreak a warning of future risks, while the report does not claim that climate change alone caused this season’s cases.

content.headline: Devon community maps sewage spills in River Dart in real time
content.shortHeadline: Local group builds live sewage-spill map for River Dart
content.standfirst: Friends of the Dart has built an online platform showing reported spills, recurring pollution sites and planned improvement work. The group says it draws together public data, while acknowledging that its picture may be incomplete or contain inaccuracies.

image.caption: A kayak operator says the River Hub could help identify safer times and places to enter the Dart.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s shocking really’: Devon community tracks River Dart sewage spills

segments.body: Friends of the Dart’s River Hub brings together information about sewage spills in the River Dart, including current and recent discharges, “dry spills” and planned remedial work. The group says some public data was difficult to find and that it used freedom-of-information requests to fill gaps.

segments.title: A tool for residents
segments.body: Local residents described falling ill after swimming, though the report does not establish that the river caused those illnesses. A kayak operator said the platform could help him judge when and where it is safer to take clients on the river. Friends of the Dart is offering its model to other communities.

segments.title: Responses and limitations
segments.body: The group says its data may be incomplete or inaccurate and invites corrections. South West Water says its own site provides near-real-time overflow information and investment details. The Environment Agency says all storm overflows are monitored and points to planned investment and enforcement.

content.headline: Experts warn Denmark may breach conventions by delaying citizenship for statelss
content.shortHeadline: Stateless children’s citizenship cases remain on hold
content.standfirst: Experts say a prolonged pause in decisions could breach international obligations to children born stateless in Denmark. The government is reviewing whether applicants should be screened for anti-democratic views, leaving affected families uncertain about when their cases will be considered.

image.caption: A report estimates 231 stateless children born in Denmark could be affected.

sources.originalTitle: Eksperter: Danmark bryder konventioner, hvis 231 bestemte børn ikke får statsborgerskab

segments.body: DR reports that 72 stateless children born in Denmark met the requirements for citizenship in January and were included in a bill that fell after an election. Their cases are now on hold while the government considers screening applicants for anti-democratic views. DR’s records indicate as many as 231 stateless children born in Denmark may be affected.

segments.title: Legal concerns
segments.body: Senior researcher Eva Ersbøll says stateless children born in Denmark have a right to citizenship and that a long suspension of decisions may conflict with the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. Immigration-law specialist Jytte Lindgård says the issue depends partly on how long the pause lasts and whether already assessed cases are reopened.

segments.title: No timetable yet
segments.body: The report says parliament may not consider screening applicants until next year. As children grow older, they may face stricter citizenship requirements. The immigration ministry said it is processing certain applications but did not provide an interview or clarify the status of cases previously recommended for approval.

content.headline: Greenland’s Kujalleq municipality suspends alcohol sales and service
content.shortHeadline: Alcohol sales and service suspended in Kujalleq
content.standfirst: The Greenlandic government has imposed a temporary ban at the municipality’s request, citing children’s welfare and public safety after alcohol-related incidents. The order does not say how long the restriction will last.

image.caption: Narsaq is one of the towns in Kujalleq, where alcohol sales have been suspended.

sources.originalTitle: Alkohol forbydes i grønlandsk kommune for befolkningens sikkerhed
Grønlandsk kommune stopper salg af alkohol

segments.body: Greenland’s government has temporarily banned the sale and serving of alcohol in Kujalleq, in the south of the country, after the municipal council requested it. The government said the measure is intended to protect children and public safety, referring to fatal incidents linked to alcohol.

segments.title: Duration not specified
segments.body: Mayor Malene Vahl Rasmussen said the community could no longer remain passive about the effects of alcohol use. The restriction took effect on Friday and remains in force until the order is repealed; authorities have not said when that might be.

segments.title: Previous restrictions
segments.body: The reports note that alcohol restrictions have been used in parts of Greenland before. During the coronavirus pandemic, sales of drinks above 2.25% alcohol were temporarily restricted in several locations, with authorities then citing the need to protect children at home.

content.headline: Aarhus residents plan evening walks after assaults; police warn against patrols
content.shortHeadline: Police warn against private patrols after Aarhus assaults
content.standfirst: Residents have organised group walks after two reported assaults on women near Riis Skov. Police say the cases may be connected but it is too early to know, and warn residents not to set up anything resembling a private patrol.

image.caption: Police say it is too early to know whether the assaults near Riis Skov are connected.

sources.originalTitle: Politiet efterforsker, om overfald på unge kvinder ved Risskov kan hænge sammen
Overfald på kvindelige løbere får Jacob til at samle bekymrede naboer til aftenture i skoven
Politi fraråder på det kraftigste ny patruljegruppe

segments.body: East Jutland Police are investigating whether two assaults on women near Riis Skov in Aarhus are connected. A 22-year-old was allegedly knocked down and assaulted in July; a 24-year-old reported being pushed down and held in September. Police say it is too early to establish a link.

segments.title: Residents’ response
segments.body: Local residents have organised evening walks in small groups after the incidents. One organiser described the aim as being present and helping if someone is attacked, rather than acting as a formal security force. The reports differ on the organiser’s surname; this account identifies him simply as a local resident.

segments.title: Police advice
segments.body: Police strongly discourage private patrols, saying officers have the authority and resources to handle suspects and that informal groups could make people feel less safe. They say extra officers will be visible in the area and advise anyone who feels unsafe to arrange to walk with others and report suspicious activity.

content.headline: Danish justice minister seeks proposals to bar prosecutors’ religious symbols
content.shortHeadline: Danish minister seeks ban on prosecutors’ religious symbols
content.standfirst: Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen has asked officials to propose a rule barring prosecutors from wearing religious or political symbols in court. Supporters say it would reinforce neutrality; the proposal has not yet become law.

image.caption: Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen has asked for proposals on symbols worn by prosecutors.

sources.originalTitle: Politikere vil forbyde anklagere at bære religiøse symboler

segments.body: Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen has asked his ministry to prepare proposals for prohibiting prosecutors from wearing religious or political symbols in court. Existing rules bar judges and lay judges from wearing such symbols during hearings.

segments.title: Supporters cite impartiality
segments.body: Social Democrats and the Socialist People’s Party support extending the restrictions to prosecutors, arguing that court proceedings should appear neutral and free from doubt about political or religious influence. The debate followed a prosecutor’s announcement that she would be Denmark’s first prosecutor to wear a headscarf.

segments.title: Proposal still to come
segments.body: The gathered report does not include a final draft or timetable for legislation. A law student quoted by DR said she was tired of the debate over whether prosecutors should be allowed to wear a headscarf; the report ends before giving her full response.

content.headline: Danish music sector warns political pressure could threaten artistic freedom
content.shortHeadline: Music industry warns against political pressure on festivals
content.standfirst: Music figures say threats to withdraw municipal funding after controversial bookings could pressure venues to self-censor. Local politicians retain a role in setting funding frameworks, but a Local Government Denmark representative says they should respect the arm’s-length principle.

image.caption: Musician Isam B has been at the centre of recent disputes over cultural programming.

sources.originalTitle: 'Det er jo noget, vi ser i autoritære regimer': Musikbranche bekymret for politisk indblanding

segments.body: Music over Præstø Fjord lost municipal support for next year’s programme after controversy over booking Isam B, according to DR. The report also cites earlier disputes involving Vega and Roskilde Festival, where politicians questioned support or cooperation after contentious bookings.

segments.title: Fear of self-censorship
segments.body: Festival and venue representatives say organisations that rely heavily on local funding may avoid booking artists or programmes that attract political criticism. Musician Mattias Kolstrup said the pattern reminded him of restrictions on artistic freedom he had encountered in Russia.

segments.title: The arm’s-length principle
segments.body: Local Government Denmark’s culture committee chair said politicians may set broad funding priorities but should not interfere in which artists perform. The report notes that not everyone on the Næstved council agrees that the withdrawn support was linked to the festival’s booking.

content.headline: Student waits 13 months for disability supplement as processing delays grow
content.shortHeadline: Student waits 13 months for disability supplement decision
content.standfirst: A student with a chronic illness has waited since August 2025 for a decision on a disability supplement. Average processing can reach 15 months for some applications, despite a law intended to reduce delays.

sources.originalTitle: Hun kæmper med "usexede symptomer" og er strandet på lang venteliste

segments.body: Josefine Agnete Andersen, a 22-year-old student with ulcerative colitis, has waited 13 months for a decision on her application for a disability supplement to her student grant. She says most of her current grant goes on rent, food and transport, and worries that combining study and work could worsen her health.

segments.title: Longer queues
segments.body: The report says the average wait can reach 15 months for applications from higher-education students when more medical documentation is required; cases not needing further documentation average six months. Applications rose from about 3,000 in 2016 to about 7,500 in 2024.

segments.title: Possible impact on study
segments.body: A disability advocacy group says long waits can create financial strain and risk students dropping out. The responsible minister declined an interview; a governing-party spokesperson said the previous change to documentation requirements had not solved the delays and that he would discuss options with the minister.

content.headline: Banedanmark expands camera monitoring to reduce overhead-wire failures
content.shortHeadline: Rail cameras planned to detect overhead-wire faults sooner
content.standfirst: Banedanmark is adding eight cameras to identify damage to train current collectors and overhead wires. The agency says the system should improve reliability, but cannot guarantee that disruptions will be eliminated.

image.caption: Overhead-wire failures have caused rail delays and cancellations this year.

sources.originalTitle: Efter nedrevne køreledninger vil Banedanmark udrulle ny løsning

segments.body: Banedanmark plans to install eight cameras at selected locations to monitor trains’ current collectors for damage that could lead to overhead-wire failures. The system will alert the rail agency, which says a fault may then be addressed before it disrupts train services.

segments.title: After repeated disruption
segments.body: The expansion follows incidents this year, including damaged wires near Ringsted and Sorø that caused delays and cancellations. Banedanmark says five to seven overhead wires normally fall each year and that monitoring is already operating at four locations.

segments.title: No completion date
segments.body: The agency says the planned cameras should be enough to monitor train traffic nationwide, but has not given a date for when all will be installed. It says the system can improve operational reliability but cannot remove the risk entirely.

content.headline: Copenhagen committee to decide future of Aarhus–Copenhagen seaplane route
content.shortHeadline: Seaplane route faces loss of Copenhagen environmental approval
content.standfirst: Nordic Seaplanes could lose permission to operate from Nordre Toldbod if Copenhagen’s committee follows officials’ recommendation. The company disputes the legal interpretation and says its proposed changes would meet noise limits.

image.caption: The seaplane route between Copenhagen and Aarhus opened in 2016.

sources.originalTitle: Vandfly kan snart være fortid

segments.body: Copenhagen’s Climate, Environment and Technology Committee is due to consider whether to refuse permanent environmental approval for Nordic Seaplanes’ base at Nordre Toldbod. If the recommendation is accepted, the company could lose its approval when its current permit expires on 1 January 2027.

segments.title: Company disputes assessment
segments.body: Nordic Seaplanes director and pilot Lasse Rungholm says officials have interpreted the rules incorrectly. He says the company proposed extending its floating pier by 12 metres to meet noise limits and argues the actual noise reaching land is below permitted levels.

segments.title: Support and opposition
segments.body: Some Copenhagen politicians support retaining the route and point to its potential contribution to electric seaplanes. Others say the harbour should prioritise bathing and public use without aircraft noise or emissions. The municipality had not responded to the company’s criticism when the report was published.

content.headline: Hayley Kiyoko turns Girls Like Girls into a film about queer joy
content.shortHeadline: Hayley Kiyoko brings Girls Like Girls to the big screen
content.standfirst: A decade after her breakthrough song, Kiyoko has co-written and directed a feature inspired by its story. She talks about queer and Asian representation, the film’s accepting father figure and making art in a hostile political climate.

image.caption: Hayley Kiyoko.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s radical to release a film called Girls Like Girls in this climate’: hitmaker turned director Hayley Kiyoko on sexuality, safety and becoming ‘Lesbian Jesus’

segments.body: Kiyoko says the 2015 song and video helped her feel more confident in her sexuality after she saw how many listeners shared her experience. The feature film expands that story into a love letter to her teenage self, following two girls discovering their feelings for each other.

segments.title: Representation and queer joy
segments.body: Kiyoko wanted the film’s central romance to reflect both queer experience and her Asian heritage. She says she rarely saw stories like her own on cinema screens growing up. In the current political climate, she sees releasing a film called Girls Like Girls as a way to affirm that queer stories and love matter.

content.headline: Erasure’s 40-year friendship carries them through grief and a new album
content.shortHeadline: Erasure’s friendship endures as Vince Clarke steps back
content.standfirst: Andy Bell and Vince Clarke reflect on four decades together, the bereavements that deepened their bond and Radio!! Radio!!. Clarke will direct the band’s coming tour remotely, following his wife’s death.

image.caption: Vince Clarke and Andy Bell.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s a deep soul connection’: Erasure on how 40 years of friendship got them through grief – and why Vince Clarke has quit touring

segments.body: Bell and Clarke describe a friendship that has helped them support one another through the deaths of their partners. Their new album, Radio!! Radio!!, emerged from difficult years; Clarke says Bell gave him the love and support he needed after his wife Tracy died in 2024.

segments.title: A different kind of tour
segments.body: For the first time in Erasure’s history, Clarke will not perform on the band’s arena tour. He will serve as musical director remotely, with keyboard technician Howard Rider playing the synthesizers on stage. Bell admits he is apprehensive about touring without his longtime partner.

segments.title: Pop, camp and solidarity
segments.body: Bell says the album’s song “Holy!” speaks to LGBTQ+ communities facing renewed attacks, while the pair discuss how Erasure’s camp performance style challenged expectations. Bell’s view is that music’s best response to hostility and grief is to bring people together.

content.headline: Liz Harris finds renewal in Helen after a viral streaming scam
content.shortHeadline: Grouper’s Liz Harris on streaming scams and bandmate connection
content.standfirst: A viral Grouper song brought new listeners—and fraudsters trying to claim its royalties. Harris explains why the experience reinforced her wariness of the music business, and how making a new Helen album made collaboration feel restorative.

image.caption: Liz Harris of Helen and Grouper.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s rational to fear the music industry’: Grouper’s Liz Harris on virality, streaming scammers and her ‘restorative’ dream-pop trio

segments.body: Harris says Grouper’s “Poison Tree” was fraudulently uploaded and registered by someone else after it gained traction on TikTok, earning around six figures before she and her label manager were able to shut down the scam and recover what she was owed. She says fake remixes and copycat uploads continue to demand time from independent artists.

segments.title: A different kind of music-making
segments.body: Harris’s new album with the dream-pop trio Helen brings a brightness and collectivity she says she does not find in Grouper’s more solitary work. Practising with friends helped lift her spirits while she was dealing with medical difficulties; she calls the process restorative.

segments.title: Making room for a full life
segments.body: The interview traces how Harris’s DIY outlook, side projects and older songs have shaped her relationship with work and performance. She describes “Poison Tree” finding a much larger audience as strange, but welcomes younger listeners discovering her music.

content.headline: Venom’s Cronos brought danger back to metal and inspired black metal
content.shortHeadline: Cronos made Venom sound dangerous—and helped shape black metal
content.standfirst: Conrad “Cronos” Lant, who died aged 63, led Venom with a raw, theatrical sound that helped give black metal its name. His influence reached far beyond the band’s modest chart success.

image.caption: Cronos of Venom in 1985.

sources.originalTitle: Conrad ‘Cronos’ Lant, frontman of UK heavy metal band Venom, dies aged 63
No one could terrify like Cronos, the black metal innovator who reignited rock’s hellraising attitude

segments.body: Lant joined the Newcastle band Venom as a teenager, eventually becoming its singer and bassist. Under the name Cronos, he paired a hoarse vocal and forceful stage presence with occult imagery and fast, abrasive music. The band’s album Black Metal gave a name to one of heavy music’s most influential subgenres.

segments.title: Influence without endorsement
segments.body: Venom’s raw, unruly sound influenced thrash and black metal musicians, but Lant objected to the violence associated with parts of the Norwegian black metal scene. He told the Quietus it was a shame those musicians were known for violence rather than their music.

segments.title: The showman behind the legend
segments.body: The obituary records Lant’s departure and later return to Venom, as well as the band’s DIY origins and his pride in making music unlike more polished early-1980s metal. A statement from Venom said his voice, bass and vision had been at the heart of the band for more than four decades. No cause of death was given.

content.headline: Soft Cell’s final album became a farewell after Dave Ball’s death
content.shortHeadline: Marc Almond reflects on Soft Cell’s final album with Dave Ball
content.standfirst: Marc Almond and Dave Ball finished Danceteria two days before Ball died in 2025. Almond discusses the record as a closing chapter, their early success and the New York nightlife that shaped Soft Cell.

image.caption: Marc Almond and Dave Ball of Soft Cell.

sources.originalTitle: Soft Cell’s Marc Almond: ‘We finished the album – two days later Dave passed away’

segments.body: Almond says he would not make another Soft Cell album without Ball, his musical partner for nearly 50 years. Danceteria, released after Ball’s death, revisits the pair’s early-1980s experiences in New York and becomes their sixth and final album.

segments.title: A city and a closing chapter
segments.body: The album looks back to a New York scene of underground clubs and creative freedom, but Almond also recalls how the AIDS crisis changed the city and its nightlife. He says he and Ball had grown closer while making the record and is relieved they completed it together.

content.headline: This week’s new tracks find beauty in Heavensouls’ breakneck sound
content.shortHeadline: Heavensouls turns breakneck chaos into a beautiful new sound
content.standfirst: Chidi Obialo’s Cantu of the Sower moves from glittering textures to crunching bass and brass. The weekly playlist also highlights new work by Mei Semones, Angèle, Romy Mars and others.

image.caption: Chidi Obialo, who records as Heavensouls.

sources.originalTitle: Add to playlist: the beautiful, breakneck chaos of Heavensouls and the week’s best new tracks

segments.body: Heavensouls’ six-song Cantu of the Sower turns rapid stylistic shifts and overloaded rhythms into something the reviewer finds absorbing rather than abrasive. Chidi Obialo’s collages mix playful detail with found sounds and a sample of civil rights activist Stokely Carmichael.

segments.title: More to queue up
segments.body: The week’s other picks range from Mei Semones’s bossa nova-inflected song about unrequited love to Angèle’s electroclash collaboration with Caroline Polachek and SebastiAn. The selection also includes new tracks by Romy Mars, Madra Salach, Blackhaine, Ryley Walker and Hodge.

content.headline: Rubber Soul’s deluxe reissue reveals an album that was never fixed in place
content.shortHeadline: The Beatles’ Rubber Soul remains in flux on its deluxe reissue
content.standfirst: The expanded edition brings together different national releases, mixes and outtakes, tracing the Beatles’ creative leap while showing how recording, commerce and listeners shaped the album.

sources.originalTitle: Rubber Soul (Super Deluxe)

segments.body: The review treats Rubber Soul as a pivotal album made under pressure: the Beatles completed it quickly while beginning to imagine records as works beyond a collection of singles. Its songs brought folk, R&B, pop and studio experimentation into close conversation.

segments.title: More than one Rubber Soul
segments.body: The set includes the UK and US track lists, stereo and mono mixes, outtakes and a new mix. Those versions expose different choices and possibilities, the review argues, rather than revealing one definitive album. Its extras offer a portrait of young musicians working out what they wanted to make.

content.headline: Elvis Costello’s debut box set traces the making of My Aim Is True
content.shortHeadline: A new box set charts how Elvis Costello found his voice
content.standfirst: The 104-track anniversary edition follows Costello from early demos to the sound of his 1977 debut. The review finds a gradual transformation behind what once looked like an out-of-nowhere arrival.

sources.originalTitle: My Aim Is True (49th Anniversary Edition)

segments.body: The review hears My Aim Is True as a vivid debut: sharp, catchy songs carrying social and romantic grievance, with an unruly wit. The box set’s demos and early recordings complicate the idea that Costello arrived fully formed, revealing a songwriter developing his craft over time.

segments.title: A transformation in stages
segments.body: The collection follows Costello through pub rock, early solo recordings and the sessions that shaped the album’s sound. The reviewer finds its early discs especially illuminating, while the later live material is more a pleasure for devoted fans than an essential part of the story.

content.headline: Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall turns a concert into an intimate film
content.shortHeadline: Paul Thomas Anderson captures Cameron Winter in concert
content.standfirst: Shot on 35mm, Paul Thomas Anderson’s 75-minute film preserves the stark songs, close attention and collective quiet of Winter’s Carnegie Hall performance. It offers little beyond the concert for viewers unfamiliar with him.

image.caption: A still from Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall.

sources.originalTitle: Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall review – Paul Thomas Anderson’s sumptuous recording is an immediate classic

segments.body: Anderson and his camera crew keep the focus on Winter’s solo performance, using close shots, shadows and carefully composed images rather than interviews or narration. The film preserves the concert’s spare setting and the attention of an audience largely absorbed in the music.

segments.title: A film for the already converted
segments.body: The reviewer praises the way the film captures Winter’s unusual voice and the quiet between songs, while noting that the concert’s communal moments do not all translate to screen. With no explanatory material or crowd work, the film is principally for viewers already drawn to his music.

content.headline: Bassam Tariq turns a stalled Blade project into a personal thriller
content.shortHeadline: Bassam Tariq finds new freedom after leaving Blade
content.standfirst: Mahershala Ali plays a devout Muslim and contract killer in Tariq’s Houston-set film. The director explains how ideas and action work from an abandoned Blade project were reshaped into a story about faith and fatherhood.

image.caption: Bassam Tariq at the Toronto Film Festival in September 2026.

sources.originalTitle: How Bassam Tariq pivoted from stalled Blade reboot to new Mahershala Ali thriller: ‘I’m happier I made this movie’

segments.body: Tariq’s film follows Latif, a father who sees his work as a contract killer through the lens of religious justice. The director says the sword in the film reflects a code that forces its user to strike with intention; the story brings faith, grief and violence into a portrait of Houston’s communities.

segments.title: What survived from Blade
segments.body: Tariq says he and Ali had prepared action sequences for the long-delayed Blade project, which he left in 2022. They carried some of that work into this more personal film. He says he is happier with the freedom of the project, while describing the earlier film’s lack of a script as a reason it stalled.

segments.title: A story rooted in fatherhood
segments.body: The film’s opening crisis draws on Tariq’s experience searching for breast milk after his wife was hospitalised following the birth of their first child. He says the experience made him confront anger at divinity and the importance of being present as a father.

content.headline: A new Sense and Sensibility finds modern tensions in Austen’s sisters
content.shortHeadline: Sense and Sensibility still speaks to modern dilemmas
content.standfirst: Georgia Oakley’s darker adaptation is uneven, but its contrasting sisters offer a fresh way into Austen’s questions about emotion, restraint and security in an uncertain world.

image.caption: Daisy Edgar-Jones as Elinor Dashwood in Sense and Sensibility.

sources.originalTitle: Every millennial should read Sense and Sensibility

segments.body: The film follows Elinor and Marianne Dashwood as their family loses its fortune and marriage becomes a route to security. The review finds the adaptation hit and miss, but argues that Austen’s two sisters remain a sharp lens on how people balance feeling with restraint.

segments.title: Austen for the social-media age
segments.body: The reviewer connects the sisters’ opposing temperaments to contemporary pressures to disclose everything while maintaining a polished public self. Marianne’s romance with Willoughby, a charming man who leaves his intentions uncertain, is read as a familiar lesson in overlooking red flags.

content.headline: James Dean’s vulnerability mattered more than his rebellious image
content.shortHeadline: The vulnerable James Dean behind the icon
content.standfirst: A new television adaptation of East of Eden prompts a look back at Dean’s defining film role. The story argues that his appeal lay not only in youthful rebellion but in the vulnerability visible beneath the myth.

image.caption: James Dean on the set of Giant in 1955.

sources.originalTitle: The truth about James Dean

segments.body: Dean’s performance as Cal in Elia Kazan’s East of Eden helped establish the actor as an emblem of restless youth. The article recalls Kazan’s unconventional direction and the intense, unpredictable quality he saw in Dean’s work, which resisted easy comparison with Marlon Brando.

segments.title: A short career, a lasting image
segments.body: Dean died at 24 after making three starring films, two released after his death. The article weighs the iconography of the red jacket and the famous photographs against the rawness of his screen presence, ending with the moment Cal reaches for his distant father.

content.headline: Brassed Off at 30: Mark Herman says its story still resonates
content.shortHeadline: Why Brassed Off still speaks to audiences 30 years on
content.standfirst: The writer-director reflects on the comedy-drama’s unexpectedly broad audience, its political roots and the difficulty of getting mid-budget British films made today.

image.caption: Pete Postlethwaite in Brassed Off.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I thought Brassed Off might be popular within a 10 mile radius of Barnsley’: the director of Andy Burnham’s favourite film on its 30 year anniversary

segments.body: Herman expected Brassed Off, about a South Yorkshire colliery band facing the closure of its pit, to find an audience close to its setting. Instead, the film’s blend of comedy and politics travelled widely. He says its lasting appeal comes from the universal experience of people feeling downtrodden.

segments.title: The shrinking space for British films
segments.body: Herman says he has spent years trying to get similar films made, but sees little room between blockbusters and micro-budget projects. On the anniversary, the real Grimethorpe Colliery Band is due to perform the music at the Royal Albert Hall alongside a screening.

content.headline: Digger’s eco-satire is ambitious but loses its way, review says
content.shortHeadline: Digger’s eco-satire has striking images but little depth
content.standfirst: Alejandro G Iñárritu’s film gives Tom Cruise a loud role as an oil tycoon, but the review finds its satire glib and its storytelling undermined by a late narrative turn.

image.caption: Tom Cruise as Digger Rockwell in Digger.

sources.originalTitle: Digger review – Tom Cruise’s loudmouth oil tycoon goes hard in Alejandro G Iñárritu’s eco-satire

segments.body: Cruise plays Digger Rockwell, an oil executive whose company’s drilling triggers a crisis when a vast ice floe breaks away in the Arctic. The review praises some of the film’s disturbing imagery and Cruise’s boisterous performance, but calls the satire shallow and laborious.

segments.title: A twist that weakens the argument
segments.body: The review says a major shift in the story makes it harder to invest in the crisis the film has been building. It sees the film’s engagement with climate catastrophe as relevant, but argues that its broad characterisations and unchallenged claims leave the satire less incisive than it might have been.

content.headline: Why horror films keep bending themselves to awards categories
content.shortHeadline: The Golden Globes leave horror with an awkward choice
content.standfirst: The team behind Obsession is submitting the violent horror film as a comedy. The choice illustrates how the Globes’ genre divisions can leave successful horror films struggling to compete.

image.caption: A still from Obsession.

sources.originalTitle: Horror films like Obsession are shut out of the Golden Globes – unless they pretend to be comedies

segments.body: The Golden Globes divide major film categories between drama and musical or comedy, leaving horror with no natural fit. Obsession, a dark story of a man using a magical trinket to make a woman love him, is being submitted in the comedy category despite its violent plot.

segments.title: A strategic route to recognition
segments.body: The article argues that horror is often treated as too genre-driven for drama awards, while comedy categories may offer a more attainable path. It notes that category placement can affect campaign momentum, and that Obsession’s lead performance could be its strongest awards prospect.

content.headline: Star Wars risks returning to a Skywalker story it has already ended
content.shortHeadline: A new Skywalker trilogy would take Star Wars backward
content.standfirst: Reports that Jon Watts may direct a new trilogy have few confirmed details, but the prospect raises a larger question: can the franchise move forward without reviving its central family saga?

image.caption: Daisy Ridley as Rey in The Rise of Skywalker.

sources.originalTitle: A new Skywalker trilogy for Star Wars? Going back to the same family-saga well is a waste of time

segments.body: A report says Lucasfilm has hired Jon Watts to direct the first film in a possible new trilogy written by Simon Kinberg, with Daisy Ridley reportedly being considered to return as Rey. The films have not been greenlit, and few further details are available.

segments.title: The case for leaving the saga behind
segments.body: The writer argues that Star Wars has repeatedly tried to conclude the Skywalker story and that its most interesting recent projects have explored other corners of the galaxy. The challenge, the piece suggests, is not simply to bring familiar characters back but to make room for stories that can end.

content.headline: The Celebrity Traitors’ Richard E Grant turns a blunder into a new game
content.shortHeadline: Richard E Grant’s Traitors confession changes the game
content.standfirst: Grant told the other contestants he was a traitor almost immediately after being selected. Reviews differ on whether the lapse has made the series better television, but agree it puts him under intense scrutiny.

image.caption: Richard E Grant and Maya Jama, the show’s initial traitors.

sources.originalTitle: The Celebrity Traitors review – Ross Kemp really needs to get a grip
Richard E Grant has already ruined The Celebrity Traitors. It’s brilliant
Richard E Grant has one hope of lasting on Celebrity Traitors: leaning into his eccentricity

segments.body: In the opening episode, Grant was chosen as a traitor and then told Joe Lycett that he was one. The other contestants had to decide whether to believe him, while Grant and fellow traitor Maya Jama faced the task of keeping suspicion from settling on them.

segments.title: A mistake, or television gold?
segments.body: The i Paper’s review calls the disclosure a spectacular cock-up that could define the series; the Guardian’s analysis sees Grant forced to lean into his eccentricity if he is to survive. Both identify the same risk: drawing attention to himself could make him an early target.

perspectives.body: The i Paper’s review relishes how Grant’s blunder has reshaped the show and argues that the unexpected confession could make an already familiar format feel newly unpredictable.

content.headline: Doctor Who’s future is uncertain after the Disney+ partnership ends
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who faces an uncertain future after Disney+ exit
content.standfirst: The BBC has ended its co-production with Disney+, cancelled a planned Christmas special and is seeking another funding partner. Fans and former contributors disagree about what went wrong, while the next Doctor remains unknown.

image.caption: Several actors who have played the Doctor.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: Since the 2025 series ended with Ncuti Gatwa’s departure, Doctor Who has had no announced replacement Doctor. The BBC has ended its partnership with Disney+ and cancelled a planned Christmas special; it is seeking a new production partner, but none has yet been confirmed.

segments.title: A format built on change
segments.body: The series has weathered earlier pauses by changing actors and showrunners, a cycle that fans and television historians describe as part of its appeal. Some contributors blame confusing scripts or the limits of a costly international partnership; others say the show’s central values and long history leave room for a return.

content.headline: Youth asks whether TV lets women in their 50s be ordinary
content.shortHeadline: Youth’s beautiful lead raises a question about TV’s beauty rules
content.standfirst: Sharon Horgan’s new sex comedy gives her a complicated midlife role, but a review argues that her glamour undercuts its claim to everywoman relatability—and points to wider double standards on screen.

image.caption: Sharon Horgan in Youth.

sources.originalTitle: Sharon Horgan’s Youth has one big problem

segments.body: Horgan plays Alex, a 50-something literary agent caught between work, an adolescent son and ageing parents. The review praises the premise and Horgan’s writing, while questioning whether audiences can identify with a character presented as an everywoman when her performer is so conventionally beautiful.

segments.title: Who gets to look ordinary?
segments.body: The piece argues that women on television are still held to narrower appearance standards than men, even as stories about their emotional lives have grown more complex. It frames its criticism as a challenge to casting norms, rather than a complaint about Horgan’s performance or ambition.

content.headline: Lenny Rush leads a vampire comedy about the awkwardness of belonging
content.shortHeadline: Lenny Rush finds his place in The Reluctant Vampire
content.standfirst: Rush stars as a young man in a vampire family who cannot stand the sight of blood. He discusses comedy, disability and a role that turns teenage feelings of not fitting in into supernatural farce.

image.caption: Lenny Rush as Val in The Reluctant Vampire.

sources.originalTitle: Fangs a million: Lenny Rush on turning an Eric Morecambe classic into a hilarious vampire comedy

segments.body: The Reluctant Vampire adapts Eric Morecambe’s 1980s children’s book, with Rush playing Val, a supposed vampire who dislikes blood and turns out to be human. The Guardian describes the series as slapstick mixed with pathos, written by the team behind Alan Partridge.

segments.title: Visibility and being typecast
segments.body: Rush says messages from parents have shown him that seeing an actor with dwarfism on television can give children confidence. He also hopes not to be confined to comedy, and describes Val’s struggle to fit in as a broader story about finding a place in society.

content.headline: War turns a wealthy divorce into high-speed legal soap opera
content.shortHeadline: War makes divorce law a lavish television battleground
content.standfirst: Sienna Miller and Dominic West lead George Kay’s drama about a public split and rival teams of lawyers. The review finds it knowingly preposterous, fast-moving and very entertaining.

image.caption: James McArdle, Sienna Miller and Phoebe Fox in War.

sources.originalTitle: War review – Sienna Miller and Dominic West’s hellish divorce drama is massive, massive fun

segments.body: War centres on film star Carla Duval and social-media mogul Morgan Henderson, whose divorce draws two rival law firms into a battle over money, reputation and their marriage agreement. The Guardian’s review relishes the twists, manoeuvres and extravagant characters.

segments.title: Entertainment without homework
segments.body: The review calls the series a high-stakes drama that does not demand emotional investment, praising its brisk plotting and performances from Miller, West and the supporting cast. It treats the show’s melodrama as an intentional escape rather than a claim to realism.

content.headline: Bake Off’s Nigella Lawson pushes back against food guilt
content.shortHeadline: Nigella brings unapologetic pleasure to Bake Off
content.standfirst: Lawson’s enjoyment of the contestants’ bakes is more than a judging style, argues this review: it offers a welcome contrast to calorie counting and the language of “naughty” food.

image.caption: Nigella Lawson on The Great British Bake Off.

sources.originalTitle: Nigella is dismantling skinny culture one ‘naughty cookie’ at a time

segments.body: The review celebrates Lawson’s exuberant tasting and her refusal to describe food as “naughty”. When fellow judge Paul Hollywood used the term about cookies, Lawson said people should take pleasure where they can in life.

segments.title: A different tone in the tent
segments.body: The writer contrasts Lawson’s appetite with a culture of weight-loss advertising and food guilt, and with earlier comments about whether a bake was “worth the calories”. She sees Lawson’s approach as a small but meaningful change in a mainstream programme.

content.headline: Carrie’s new adaptation has already stirred debate about casting
content.shortHeadline: Why Carrie fans are questioning the new adaptation
content.standfirst: Mike Flanagan’s series has drawn criticism for departing from Stephen King’s description of Carrie White. The debate concerns not only appearance, but how adaptations translate a character’s anger and agency.

image.caption: A still from the new Carrie adaptation.

sources.originalTitle: Why a new TV version of horror classic Carrie is already annoying people

segments.body: Some readers have objected that screen versions cast Carrie as conventionally attractive and soften the anger and physical description of King’s bullied teenager. The new series also changes her background: she has been homeschooled and enters school after her father’s death.

segments.title: Adaptation and the market
segments.body: A horror scholar sees the series’ use of social media as a way to update the story’s bullying, while another film-maker notes that casting can be shaped by production funding as well as creative choice. The article argues that the new version departs from the book, but reports that it has also drawn praise for its performances and contemporary setting.

content.headline: To Catch a Predator’s ratings success left difficult questions about TV ethics
content.shortHeadline: The TV ethics questions behind To Catch a Predator
content.standfirst: A new film revives interest in the sting show that mixed reporting, law enforcement and reality-TV spectacle. Its legacy includes questions about humiliation, consent and the consequences of the format.

image.caption: A still from the documentary about To Catch a Predator.

sources.originalTitle: How controversial 2000s paedophile-hunting show To Catch a Predator rocked US TV

segments.body: To Catch a Predator lured men who had communicated with decoys posing as teenagers to a house, where cameras recorded presenter Chris Hansen confronting them before police made arrests. The show became a ratings hit, blurring the boundaries between investigative journalism, policing and entertainment.

segments.title: The cost of spectacle
segments.body: The article examines the 2006 case in which an assistant district attorney died by suicide after a sting operation at his home, and reports on criticism of the show’s methods. Documentary-maker David Osit, himself a survivor of sexual abuse, describes the risks of turning social justice into a ratings-driven story; Hansen has disputed criticism of his work.

segments.title: A format that persists
segments.body: Although NBC cancelled the original strand in 2008, the article says similar stings continue in streaming and online video. It raises the unresolved question of how media can inform audiences without turning humiliation and punishment into entertainment.

content.headline: Gears of War: E-Day has excellent combat but little else to offer
content.shortHeadline: E-Day’s combat is strong; its campaign feels repetitive
content.standfirst: The prequel delivers the series’ most satisfying combat yet, but the review finds repeated routes, cluttered levels and too many collectibles around it.

image.caption: Marcus Fenix in Gears of War: E-Day.

sources.originalTitle: Gears of War: E-Day review – an alien invasion shouldn’t be this boring

segments.body: E-Day revisits the alien invasion that shaped the series, putting Marcus Fenix and a squad of soldiers at its centre. The Guardian finds its shooting and cover mechanics the best the games have felt, with destructible environments and weighty weapons adding force to firefights.

segments.title: A promising setting stretched thin
segments.body: The review says the campaign repeatedly sends players across the same city, with large areas crowded by collectibles and side missions. Its horror moments in enclosed spaces stand out, but the story and level design do not develop enough to sustain the prequel’s long run.

content.headline: Resident Evil succeeds by recreating what it feels like to play
content.shortHeadline: Resident Evil finds its fear in the experience of playing
content.standfirst: Zach Cregger’s adaptation leaves out the series’ familiar heroes but borrows its vulnerable protagonist, scarce ammunition and unnerving spaces to evoke the games’ particular kind of dread.

image.caption: Zach Cregger and Austin Abrams on the set of Resident Evil.

sources.originalTitle: How Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil stands out from all other game adaptations

segments.body: The film follows courier Bryan Hodukavich through a viral outbreak without weapons or a clear understanding of what is happening. Its abandoned locations, limited ammunition, found recordings and brief encounters with other characters echo the structure of the games.

segments.title: A different kind of adaptation
segments.body: Rather than retelling the familiar heroes’ stories, Cregger aims to reproduce the player’s uncertainty and vulnerability, the review argues. It connects that choice to the series’ creator Shinji Mikami’s view that horror is strongest when survival is never assured.

content.headline: Ace Combat 8 makes aerial combat feel thrilling and cinematic
content.shortHeadline: Ace Combat 8 delivers a high-flying Top Gun fantasy
content.standfirst: The review praises the game’s dramatic dogfights, accessible flying and more fully realised story, while noting that crowded missions can make objectives hard to follow.

image.caption: An aircraft in Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve.

sources.originalTitle: Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve review – brilliant aerial combat game fulfils the Top Gun fantasy

segments.body: In a fictional world where fighter planes dominate, players become a propaganda hero who must live up to the legend. The Guardian says the game makes aerial combat feel exhilarating, with varied missions, dramatic radio chatter and controls that welcome newcomers as well as series veterans.

segments.title: A story that lands
segments.body: The review says new animated first-person scenes and cinematic cutscenes give the pilot’s wing-mates and wartime drama more emotional weight. It praises the spectacle but notes that visual clutter can obscure objectives; the reviewer could not assess the online multiplayer mode during the review period.

content.headline: The Roblox scam that tricks children into giving away their accounts
content.shortHeadline: How fake Robux offers steal children’s Roblox logins
content.standfirst: Fraudulent links on video and chat platforms can lead children to convincing fake sign-in pages. Security experts advise opening Roblox directly and never sharing passwords or authentication codes.

image.caption: Roblox advises users to access the service through its official app or website.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Mum, where did my Robux go?’ The Roblox scam targeting children

segments.body: Scammers promise free Robux through links posted in YouTube or TikTok comments and Discord chats. The links can lead to lookalike pages that collect usernames, passwords and two-factor codes, then redirect children to the real Roblox site so the theft is less obvious.

segments.title: What families can do
segments.body: NordVPN advises children to open Roblox through its official app or website rather than links sent to them, and to treat authentication and backup codes like passwords. Roblox says it has security measures against phishing, but warns that lost currency or items may not be recoverable.

content.headline: A father and son return to the game that began their gaming bond
content.shortHeadline: Replaying Call of Duty brings a father and son closer
content.standfirst: After 17 years, a father and his adult son return to the co-op missions they first tried when the son was five. Their shared play becomes a story of teamwork, time and a bond that will soon change.

image.caption: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2, the game the pair played together.

sources.originalTitle: Playing video games with my 22-year-old son has brought me to tears

segments.body: The writer and his 22-year-old son replay the Special Ops missions in Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2 that they first attempted in 2009. Their approaches differ—one cautious, the other charging ahead—until they learn to coordinate and finally complete missions they once could not finish.

segments.title: The value of playing together
segments.body: The essay finds unexpected ease in gaming with his son, away from work and everyday responsibilities. Their time in the flat will not last: they are due to move to different parts of the world in a few months. The son says he will remember these sessions as some of their best times together.

content.headline: The volunteer Pokémon professors who keep tournaments running
content.shortHeadline: Meet the volunteers behind competitive Pokémon
content.standfirst: At the 2026 world championships, volunteer professors judged games, helped players and managed the event. Their roles are essential, but how they are compensated is not fully clear.

image.caption: Attendees at the 2026 Pokémon world championships in San Francisco.

sources.originalTitle: Meet the real-life Pokémon professors, the unsung heroes of competitive monster-battling

segments.body: Real-life Pokémon professors are volunteers who teach rules, judge matches and help organise tournaments. At the 2026 world championships, roughly 300 were present, according to a Pokémon Company International representative; their work ranges from technical support to making final rulings.

segments.title: The work behind the matches
segments.body: Head judge Gemma Byard describes checking results, keeping the venue safe and handling disputes. Evelyne de Groot compares the role to customer service, balancing firm rules with helping competitors enjoy the event.

segments.title: Unclear compensation
segments.body: Some professors described receiving merchandise or help with travel and accommodation, while one said US regional judges are paid. Most interviewees declined to provide details, and the Pokémon Company International declined to comment on how professors are compensated.

content.headline: Why players are pushing back against games that remove too much friction
content.shortHeadline: Players want challenge—not constant hand-holding
content.standfirst: Viral clips of Marvel’s Wolverine have revived a debate about games that highlight every path and objective. The argument is that useful guidance can become intrusive when it removes player agency.

image.caption: Marvel’s Wolverine.

sources.originalTitle: Why fans are digging their claws into Wolverine over its patronising gameplay

segments.body: The Guardian describes a wave of criticism after clips from Wolverine showed repeated cues pointing players towards objectives and collectibles. The writer argues that the issue is not difficulty alone, but “friction”: the space a game leaves for players to explore, learn and make choices.

segments.title: Room to learn
segments.body: The piece contrasts games that guide players clearly without taking over with designs that mark every ledge or have characters repeat instructions. It argues that challenge can be rewarding when players have to work out what to do, while acknowledging that guidance can prevent people getting stuck.

segments.title: A wider design debate
segments.body: The writer hopes the reaction to Wolverine reminds studios that players can enjoy uncertainty and gradual mastery. Examples including Hollow Knight: Silksong and Blue Prince show how different kinds of challenge can leave room for agency without relying on the same formula.

content.headline: Does romancing a game character count as cheating? GTA VI sparks debate
content.shortHeadline: GTA VI prompts a debate about virtual romance and cheating
content.standfirst: The game’s relationship mechanics have prompted social-media claims that playing it could be unfaithful. The article argues that the reaction also reflects real anxieties about attention and connection in relationships.

image.caption: Lucia and Jason in Grand Theft Auto VI.

sources.originalTitle: Grand Theft Auto VI: can playing a video game count as cheating on your partner?

segments.body: Players of Grand Theft Auto VI will be able to strengthen the relationship between protagonists Lucia and Jason through dates, messages and other interactions. Some social-media users say that participating in an in-game romance amounts to cheating; the article notes that the mechanic works in both directions.

segments.title: More than a game mechanic
segments.body: The writer rejects a blanket definition of virtual romance as infidelity, while arguing that people who feel neglected may understandably be hurt if a partner invests attention in a fictional relationship. The piece frames the online argument as a reflection of loneliness and dissatisfaction, not as a universal rule for couples.
